what_its_for: Niacin is a B vitamin (vitamin B3) used to help lower bad cholesterol (LDL) and triglycerides (fats in the blood) while raising good cholesterol (HDL). It is used along with diet changes and exercise to reduce the risk of heart disease.
how_to_take: Take niacin exactly as your doctor tells you. Extended-release tablets (like Niaspan) should be swallowed whole — do not crush, break, or chew them. Take niacin with a low-fat snack or meal to help reduce stomach upset. Taking an aspirin (325 mg) or ibuprofen 30 minutes before your niacin dose may help reduce flushing (redness and warmth of the skin). Do not drink alcohol or hot beverages around the time you take niacin, as this can make flushing worse. Extended-release niacin is usually taken at bedtime.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over several weeks to reduce side effects. A common starting dose is 500 mg once daily at bedtime. Your doctor may increase this to 1,000 mg to 2,000 mg per day depending on your response. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first. Do not switch between different forms of niacin (regular, extended-release, or slow-release) without your doctor's approval, as this can cause serious liver problems.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store niacin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use niacin past the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol or hot drinks close to the time you take niacin, as they can increase flushing and low blood pressure. Avoid hot showers or baths right after taking niacin for the same reason. Do not take over-the-counter niacin or vitamin supplements containing niacin without talking to your doctor first, as combining them can increase the risk of side effects. Avoid high-dose niacin if you have active liver disease, a stomach ulcer, or gout. Let your doctor know if you are taking blood pressure medications, cholesterol-lowering drugs (like statins), or diabetes medications, as niacin can interact with these.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), dark urine or severe stomach pain, muscle pain, weakness, or tenderness (especially with fever), unexplained weight loss, vision changes, irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness or fainting, or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing. Contact your doctor if you have persistent flushing, itching, or tingling that bothers you, or if your blood sugar seems poorly controlled (if you have diabetes).
when_it_works: Niacin begins to affect cholesterol levels within a few weeks, but it may take 3 to 6 months to see the full benefit. Your doctor will check your cholesterol levels and liver function with blood tests during treatment. Continue taking niacin even if you feel well, as high cholesterol usually has no symptoms. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. High-dose niacin is generally not recommended during pregnancy. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as flushing and low blood pressure. Diabetes: Niacin can raise blood sugar levels. If you have diabetes, your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medications. Kidney or liver disease: Use with caution. Niacin is not recommended if you have active liver disease. Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions before starting niacin. Children: Niacin is not usually recommended for children unless specifically directed by a doctor.
